subtype: Approach: asking a parent to remind him at night [Action]
passage: My brother Asif forgets things. Everyone in our flat knows it. So I was surprised on Tuesday when he went up to Abbu at dinner, before anyone had nagged him, and said, "Abbu, tomorrow is the science exhibition. Can you ask me at nine o'clock what I need? Ask properly, like a quiz." Abbu raised his eyebrows but said yes. At nine Abbu called from the sofa, "Quiz time. What do you need?" Asif stood very straight. "Model, the signed form, white shirt." He ran to the shelf, found the form still unsigned, and brought it over with a pen. I don't know if he was worried or just trying something new. But in the morning he left with all three.

qa.a: Abbu agreed to ask at nine o'clock.

qa.q: What might Asif have been feeling when he asked Abbu for help?

qa.q: What other approach could help Asif on ordinary school days, and why?
qa.a: He could keep a written checklist by the door, because asking Abbu works for one big day but a list helps every day.

subtype: Approach: taking turns by the clock [Action]
passage:
"Mumma! Devesh has had the tablet for an hour!"
"Forty minutes, Sudhir! You had it all morning!"
"I had it for ten minutes and then you took it!"
Sudha came in wiping her hands. "Both of you, stop. Nobody here has a clock in their head." She went to the kitchen and came back with the egg timer. "Thirty minutes each. When it rings, the tablet goes to the other person. No arguing."
"Who starts?"
"Sudhir, because he's younger."
"Not fair!"
"Devesh, your thirty starts after his."
The timer ticked on the table between them. When it rang, Sudhir groaned but handed it over. Devesh set the timer himself.

qa.q: How many minutes does each boy get with the tablet?
qa.a: Thirty minutes each.

qa.q: What was Devesh feeling when he shouted "Not fair!"?
qa.a: Devesh felt annoyed and jealous that his younger brother got to start first.

qa.q: What else could make the timer plan work even better, and why?
qa.a: The boys could take turns starting first on alternate days, because then the start order itself is fair.

qa.q: How does the timer look to Sudha?
qa.a: Sudha sees it as a way to stop the shouting, since the timer decides and she no longer has to referee.

grounding: It shows two brothers sharing one tablet with a kitchen timer so a fixed thirty minutes each settles the arguments.

subtype: Approach: taking turns by the clock [Action]
passage: My brother Jay and I used to fight about the tablet every single evening. He'd say I'd had it longer; I'd say he had. Neither of us knew. Last month I had an idea: Mummy's round kitchen timer, the one shaped like a tomato. Thirty minutes each. I twisted it to thirty and handed Jay the tablet first, to show I was being fair. "Paras bhaiya, it's ringing!" he yelled when mine was done, and I gave it back without arguing, because the tomato said so. It's strange. We still want more time. But now we fight with the timer instead of each other, and the timer never shouts back.

qa.q: What shape is the kitchen timer?
qa.a: It is shaped like a tomato.

qa.q: Why did Paras give Jay the tablet first?
qa.a: Paras wanted to show the plan was fair, probably feeling hopeful that Jay would trust it.

qa.q: How does the tomato timer look to Jay?
qa.a: Jay seems to enjoy it, yelling happily when it rings, because it gives him a clear, fair turn.

grounding: It shows two brothers using a kitchen timer to give each thirty minutes so the arguments about time stop.

subtype: Approach: grabbing it first and refusing to hand over [Pitfall]

I just didn't want to lose.

subtype: Approach: grabbing it first and refusing to hand over [Pitfall]
passage: In their village above the river, there was one television in Vidya's home, and one remote with a cracked back held together by tape. On Sunday Vidya reached it first and slid it into her kurta pocket. "I'm first, so it's mine," she said. Her little brother Dorjee grabbed at her sleeve. She held her arm up high where he couldn't reach. Their grandmother put down her spinning and asked for the remote. Vidya shook her head. Dorjee wailed. Their father came in from the fields, heard both, took the remote and put it on top of the cupboard. "When you two can share, it comes down." Vidya stared at the dark screen and felt her face go hot.

qa.q: Where did the father put the remote?
qa.a: He put it on top of the cupboard.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling as she stared at the dark screen?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hot-faced, and perhaps angry, because holding on to it had cost everyone the television.

subtype: Approach: agreeing to a plan with days for each [Thinking]
passage: The family laptop was old and slow, and the internet in their building only worked properly in the evenings. Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday are yours." "And Sunday?" "Sunday we split." Samir frowned. "Your art class is on Wednesday. You don't even use it Wednesdays." Shreya thought. "True. And your spelling test is Friday, so you'd need Thursday most." She swapped Wednesday for Thursday. "Is that fair now?" Samir counted. Three each, Sunday shared. "Fair."

subtype: Approach: agreeing to a plan with days for each [Thinking]
passage: In a flat above a bakery in Pune, Jeevan and his younger brother Akash had one game console and one television. After a week of shouting, Jeevan took a sheet of paper to the dining table. "Let's think," he said. "If we split every day, we both get twenty minutes, which is nothing. If we take whole days, we each get proper time." "But which days?" Akash asked. Jeevan pointed. "You have football on Tuesdays and Thursdays, so those should be mine. Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays, yours. Weekends, turns." Akash counted on his fingers, then crossed out Friday. "Take Friday. Saturday morning is better for me." They both signed it.

qa.a: The flat sits above a bakery in Pune.

qa.q: Why did Akash cross out Friday?
qa.a: He wanted Saturday morning instead, and felt confident enough in the plan to change it to suit himself.

subtype: Approach: writing the schedule on a shared chart [Action]
passage: Preeti, you're asking why my fridge still has that yellowed paper chart on the side. Sit, and your Vinita Nani will tell you. When I was a girl, we got our first fridge, and with it, my brother and I got our first fights about turns. Not about the fridge; about the radio on top of it. Every evening he said it was his turn, and I said it was mine, and nobody could remember. So one Sunday I took a ruler and made a table. Seven days across. His name in blue, mine in red. I stuck it to the fridge with flour paste. After that, when he said "my turn," I just pointed. The chart settled it. Nobody argued with a chart.

qa.a: Her brother may have been annoyed at first, then accepted it, since it showed his turns clearly too.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a girl, she drew a coloured weekly chart of turns and stuck it on the fridge so the siblings could check instead of argue.

subtype: Approach: writing the schedule on a shared chart [Action]
passage: The family laptop in Rehana's flat was shared by three children, and nobody could remember who had it last. Then the power cuts started, two hours every evening, and the fights got worse. On Saturday Rehana took chart paper and drew a table: days down the side, time slots across, only the hours when there was power. She gave each person a colour. Samir, who was five and couldn't read yet, got green, so he could find his own squares. She stuck it on the fridge with magnets. That evening, when the power came back, Samir ran to the fridge, put his finger on a green square, and said, "Mine." Nobody argued.

subtype: Approach: negotiating by swapping what each values [Thinking]
passage: On Friday night in their small house in Busan, Jin and his sister Dalia started the usual fight over the family computer. "I need Saturday morning," Jin said. "The online game tournament is at ten." "And I need the whole weekend for my science poster." Their mother kept chopping vegetables. Jin stopped. "Wait. When do you actually need it most?" Dalia thought. "Sunday. That's when the library pictures come back." "And I only need Saturday morning." He grinned. "So I take Saturday till twelve, and you take all of Sunday." Dalia narrowed her eyes, then held out her hand. "Deal. But Saturday afternoon's mine too." "Deal."

subtype: Approach: telling the younger one to wait forever [Pitfall]
passage: In the clinic waiting room, Mummy's phone was the only thing to play with, and Gagan had it. His little sister Lalremsiami leaned on his arm. "My turn?" "Later." She sat on her hands and watched the ceiling fan. Ten minutes. "Now?" "Later, I said. I'm on the last level." A new patient came in. The last level became another last level. Lalremsiami's lip began to shake. She walked across the room to their mother. "Gagan said later three times, and later never comes." Mummy took the phone, set it to show ten minutes, and handed it to Lalremsiami. "Then Gagan gets ten." Gagan slumped in his chair.

subtype: Approach: telling the younger one to wait forever [Pitfall]
passage: I stay next door, and I see Charan and his little sister Nikita most evenings on the shared balcony. There's one cycle between them, a small red one. On Monday I heard Nikita ask for a turn. By Wednesday she had stopped asking and just sat by the door, drawing with her finger in the dust on the floor. On Thursday she went inside and I heard her talking to their mother, her voice wobbly. Their mother came out, took the cycle and gave it to Nikita. Charan went in without a word. I don't know what he thought, but he didn't ride that evening.

subtype: Approach: changing the plan when exams come [Revision]
passage: Last month my board-style mock exams started, and I realised our TV chart was not fair any more. Every evening, from six to seven, it was my hour, but I had to study, so the TV just sat there. And Payal, my little sister, had only her half hour. She kept looking at the dark screen. I felt a bit guilty. So I said, "Payal, for the next two weeks, you take my hour too." She squealed. "But when exams finish, I get extra, okay?" I said. She thought about it very seriously. "Okay, Rajni didi, two weeks for two weeks." We wrote it on the chart in pencil. Now exams are over, and it's my turn to catch up.

qa.q: Which hour was Rajni's time on the TV chart?
qa.a: Rajni's hour was from six to seven.

qa.a: They could agree that whoever is busy lends time and gets it back later, so the chart can bend without new fights.

qa.q: How does the exam-time change look to Payal?
qa.a: Payal is delighted, squealing at the extra time, and she takes the deal seriously enough to agree to pay it back.

grounding: It shows siblings noticing their schedule becomes unfair during exams and agreeing the younger gets more time for two weeks, to balance later.

subtype: Approach: finding a game they can play together [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to decide when stuck [Revision]
passage: Rekha, your Minakshi Nani and her brother once fought for a whole month over one sewing machine. Mother's machine. I wanted it for doll clothes, he wanted it to fix his kite bag, and both of us had homework to stitch for school. We tried talking. We tried shouting. We tried taking turns by the clock, and then argued about the clock. So one evening we walked into the kitchen together, which was new, and said, "Amma, you decide. We will follow whatever you say." She put down her ladle, listened to me, listened to him, and asked what each of us really needed. Then she made a rule: school work first, toys after. We grumbled. We followed it. It worked.

qa.q: How might Amma have seen the two children walking in together?
qa.a: Amma was probably surprised and pleased that they came as a team and asked her fairly.

grounding: An elder recalls how, after failed talks, she and her brother asked their mother to make the rule and agreed to follow it.

subtype: Approach: asking a parent to decide when stuck [Revision]
